title: Modern Readings
bigQuestion: How have print, empire, science, new scholarship and the internet changed the way Muslims read the Qur'an, and what stays the same?

story.title: A Sermon in New York
story.kicker: A woman stands to give the Friday sermon in 2005, and cites the Qur'an on both sides of the argument about whether she may.
paragraphs: On a Friday in March 2005, about a hundred people gathered in a hall attached to a cathedral in New York City. They had come for Friday prayer, but the building was not a mosque. No mosque in the city had agreed to host the event, and a threat had forced a change of venue. The woman who stepped forward to deliver the *khutba*, the sermon, and then lead the prayer was Amina Wadud, a professor of Islamic studies and the author of a book called Qur'an and Woman.

Men and women stood in the same rows. Journalists lined the back wall. Outside, a small group protested, holding signs that quoted the Qur'an. Inside, Wadud's sermon quoted the Qur'an too. She spoke of Surah al-Hujurat (49), ayah 13, which says God made people into nations and tribes so that they might know one another, and that the most honored before God is the most mindful. She read it as a verse about equality before God, and she argued that nothing in the text bars a woman from leading prayer.

Her critics that week, in mosques and on websites around the world, cited the same book. They pointed to Surah al-Nisa (4), ayah 34, which describes men as maintainers of women, and to hadith reports and the rulings of the classical law schools, which for centuries had reserved the leading of mixed Friday prayer to men. Some scholars called the event a break with settled practice. A few said the classical rulings were opinions, not verses, and could be reopened.

Notice what both sides shared. Everyone cited the Qur'an. Everyone appealed to the Prophet's example. Everyone claimed the tradition. The argument was not about whether to read the text but about how, and about who has the standing to read it. That is the modern situation of tafsir in a sentence. Printing presses, colonial rule, new universities, women scholars, natural science and the internet have all pulled at the question of who interprets and by what method.

This chapter follows those changes from the nineteenth century to the present: the reformers of Cairo, the revivalists of Egypt and South Asia, a philosopher in Lahore and a professor in Chicago, the women scholars, the scientific readers and their critics, the translators, and the Qur'an on a phone screen. It ends in America, where Muslims of every background read the same text in a hundred ways.
story.think: Both sides in 2005 quoted the Qur'an. What besides the text itself was each side relying on, and why does that matter for how you read a modern argument about scripture?

lessons.title: Print, Empire and the Commentary
lessons.mainIdea: Printing, European rule and new schools changed who read the Qur'an and why, and modern commentaries answered questions the classical ones never faced.
reading: For a thousand years the Qur'an was copied by hand and taught by voice. That changed slowly. Muslim scholars long resisted printing the Qur'an, partly out of respect for the text and partly from distrust of the presses, which were run by Europeans. Muslim-run presses began in the nineteenth century, including the Bulaq press near Cairo, founded in the 1820s. In 1924 the Egyptian government issued a carefully edited printed Qur'an, based on the reading of Hafs from Asim, and that edition became the standard text across most of the Muslim world.

Print did more than multiply copies. It let a commentary reach readers who had never sat with a teacher, and it let a journal carry a verse-by-verse explanation to subscribers in Cairo, Bombay and Java in the same month. A reader with a printed Qur'an, a printed tafsir and a dictionary could form opinions without a master's permission. Historians of modern Islam describe this as a shift in authority, from the scholar's chain of teachers to the printed page and the individual reader.

The second force was *colonialism*. By 1900, Britain, France, the Netherlands and Russia ruled most Muslim lands. Their schools taught science, law and history in European terms. Christian missionaries printed criticisms of the Qur'an. Muslim reformers responded with commentaries that took up the new questions directly: Is the Qur'an compatible with modern science? Does it permit constitutional government, women's education, interest-bearing loans? The classical commentators had not asked these questions because no one had put them.

So the modern commentary looks different from a classical one. It is often shorter on grammar and longer on themes. It speaks to the general reader, not the trained scholar. It argues with Europeans as well as with earlier Muslims. And it is more likely to be written in Urdu, Turkish, Malay or English than in Arabic. Every commentator in this chapter worked inside these conditions, whether he or she embraced them or fought them.

words.d: an early Muslim-run printing press near Cairo, founded in the 1820s
the printed Qur'an issued in Egypt in 1924 that became the standard text in most of the Muslim world
rule of one country over another; by 1900 European powers governed most Muslim lands
a thinker who argued that Muslims should rethink their tradition to meet modern conditions

lessons.title: Abduh, Rida and al-Manar
lessons.mainIdea: Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida's Tafsir al-Manar read the Qur'an as guidance for reform, stressing reason, the general reader and the needs of the age.
reading: Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905) grew up in the Egyptian countryside, studied at al-Azhar in Cairo, was exiled for a time after a failed revolt against British influence, and returned to become the Grand Mufti of Egypt in 1899. He believed that Islam, rightly understood, agreed with reason and could guide a modern society. Late in life he gave public lectures on the Qur'an at al-Azhar, verse by verse, to audiences that included students, officials and journalists.

One listener was Muhammad Rashid Rida (1865–1935), a Syrian who had moved to Cairo and founded a journal called al-Manar, the lighthouse, in 1898. Rida printed Abduh's lectures in the journal, with his own additions, and after Abduh's death he continued the commentary himself. The result, known as Tafsir al-Manar, reached Surah Yusuf (12) and stopped at Rida's death in 1935. It is a modern commentary in the fullest sense: composed for print, serialized in a magazine, and addressed to the reading public.

The method has several marks. Abduh insisted that the Qur'an is a book of guidance, *hidaya*, not a textbook of grammar or law, so a commentary should show what a passage means for living. He read the Qur'an by the Qur'an, treated many isra'iliyyat as unreliable, and preferred to explain miracles in ways he thought reason could accept. He also criticized *taqlid*, blind following of earlier authorities, and called for *ijtihad*, fresh reasoning from the sources. Rida shared this program but grew more cautious and more attached to hadith over time.

Historians call Abduh and Rida the founders of modernist tafsir, and nearly every later reformer answered them. Conservative scholars accused them of bending the text to please Europeans. Later liberals said they had not gone far enough. Both criticisms show their influence. The questions al-Manar raised, about reason, reform and the reader's own responsibility, are the questions the rest of this chapter follows.

words.d: Egyptian reformer (1849–1905), Grand Mufti of Egypt, whose lectures on the Qur'an began Tafsir al-Manar
Syrian-born scholar (1865–1935) who founded the journal al-Manar and completed Abduh's commentary as far as Surah 12
following earlier authorities without fresh reasoning; a practice reformers criticized
independent reasoning from the sources of Islam; reformers called for its revival

look.title: Guidance, Not Grammar
look.text: Abduh told his students that the earlier commentators had buried the Qur'an under grammar, rhetoric, legal detail and unreliable stories, and that the reader should ask first what a passage teaches about how to live. A defender of the classical commentaries replied that without grammar and reports, a reader has only his own feelings to go on, and calls them guidance.
look.prompt: State each side's strongest point. What does a reader lose by skipping the classical tools, and what does a reader lose by never getting past them?

lessons.title: Qutb and Maududi
lessons.mainIdea: Sayyid Qutb and Abul A'la Maududi wrote commentaries that read the Qur'an as a program for society and politics, and their books shaped Islamist movements.
reading: Two of the most widely read commentaries of the twentieth century came not from professional scholars but from activists. Sayyid Qutb (1906–1966) was an Egyptian teacher and literary critic who joined the Muslim Brotherhood after a stay in the United States around 1949. Abul A'la Maududi (1903–1979) was a journalist in British India who founded the Jamaat-e-Islami in 1941 and later worked in Pakistan. Both wrote for ordinary readers, and both read the Qur'an as a call to build a society governed by God's law.

Qutb's Fi zilal al-Qur'an, In the Shade of the Qur'an, was written largely in prison, where the Egyptian government held him for most of the years between 1954 and his execution in 1966. It is a commentary of feeling and of argument rather than of grammar. Qutb read the Meccan surahs as a struggle between faith and *jahiliyya*, a word that classically means the age of ignorance before Islam. He applied it to his own society, arguing that a state that does not rule by God's law is in a new jahiliyya. The idea that judgment belongs to God alone, which he drew from verses such as Surah Yusuf (12), ayah 40, became his political principle.

Maududi's Tafhim al-Qur'an, Toward Understanding the Qur'an, was written in Urdu between 1942 and 1972. It is calmer in tone and more systematic, with long introductions to each surah and many notes on law. Maududi held that the Qur'an sets out a complete system for personal, social and political life, and he coined the phrase Islamic state to describe its goal. His commentary was translated into English and many other languages and became a standard text for Islamist movements in South Asia and beyond.

Both men have been read in opposite ways. Some Muslims treasure their commentaries for their clarity and moral urgency. Many Muslim scholars reject their political readings, arguing that the classical tradition never applied jahiliyya to Muslim societies or made the state the goal of the text. Historians note that the two commentaries show how a reading of the Qur'an, printed and widely sold, could become a political program, for better or worse, in the age of the nation-state.

words.d: Egyptian writer (1906–1966) whose In the Shade of the Qur'an, written largely in prison, read the text as a struggle against a new jahiliyya
South Asian thinker (1903–1979) whose Urdu commentary Tafhim al-Qur'an presented the text as a complete system for life and state
classically, the age of ignorance in Arabia before Islam; Qutb applied the word to modern societies
describing movements that seek a state and society governed by their reading of Islamic law

lessons.title: Fazlur Rahman's Double Movement
lessons.mainIdea: Fazlur Rahman, teaching in Chicago, proposed reading each ruling in its seventh-century context to find its principle, then applying that principle to the present.
reading: Fazlur Rahman (1919–1988) was born in what is now Pakistan, studied at Oxford, and led Pakistan's Central Institute of Islamic Research in the 1960s. Opposition to his views drove him abroad, and in 1969 he joined the University of Chicago, where he taught until his death. His students there included many of the scholars who shaped Qur'anic studies in American universities. His books, especially Islam and Modernity (1982) and Major Themes of the Qur'an (1980), set out a method he called the double movement.

The first movement goes from the present back to the seventh century. A reader takes a Qur'anic ruling and studies the situation it addressed in Arabia: the customs, the problems, the reasons the verse gives. From that study the reader draws out the principle, the moral aim the ruling served. The second movement returns to the present. The reader asks what that principle requires in today's conditions, which may differ from Arabia's. The ruling's letter belongs to its time; its aim, Rahman argued, is what binds.

His favorite example concerned polygamy. Surah al-Nisa (4), ayah 3, permits marriage to up to four women but adds that if a man fears he cannot deal justly, he should marry only one. Ayah 129 of the same surah says men will never be able to deal equally between wives, however much they wish. Rahman read the permission as a concession to a society with many war orphans and widows, and the justice clause as the principle. In modern conditions, he concluded, the principle points toward monogamy. Critics replied that he was letting the reader decide which verses are principle and which are concession.

Rahman also argued that the classical scholars had treated the Qur'an as a list of separate rulings rather than a unified message with an ethical center. That charge was not new, but his method for answering it, with its explicit two-step, became one of the most discussed proposals in modern Muslim thought. Scholars in Indonesia, Turkey, South Africa and the United States adapted it, and the Chicago connection makes him a figure worth knowing for readers in Illinois.

words.d: Pakistani-born scholar (1919–1988) who taught at the University of Chicago from 1969 and proposed the double movement
Rahman's method: from the present to the Qur'an's original context to find a principle, then from the principle back to the present
the moral aim a ruling served in its setting, which Rahman argued is what binds later readers
the circumstances in which a text was first spoken or written

lessons.title: Iqbal and Reconstruction
lessons.mainIdea: Muhammad Iqbal, poet and philosopher, read the Qur'an as a call to dynamic thought and human effort, and urged Muslims to reconstruct their religious ideas.
reading: Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938) was born in Sialkot in the Punjab, studied philosophy in Cambridge and Munich, practiced law in Lahore, and became the most celebrated Urdu and Persian poet of his age. In 1930 he also gave the presidential address to the All-India Muslim League in which he proposed a separate Muslim state in northwest India, an idea later linked to the founding of Pakistan. But Iqbal is in this chapter for his reading of the Qur'an.

In a series of lectures published as The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam (1930, expanded 1934), Iqbal argued that the Qur'an's spirit is dynamic, not static. He pointed to its constant appeal to nature and history as signs, and to verses such as Surah al-Ra'd (13), ayah 11, which says God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. For Iqbal this was the Qur'an's principle of movement. He believed Muslims had frozen their law and thought, and he called for a new ijtihad using modern knowledge.

Iqbal's reading of the Qur'an drew on the Sufi tradition, especially Rumi, and on European philosophers such as Bergson and Nietzsche. He read the story of Adam's fall not as a disaster but as the birth of free choice and self-awareness, a step up rather than a step down. He saw in the Qur'an a picture of the human being as God's partner in an unfinished creation. Theologians of the classical schools did not always recognize their Qur'an in his.

Iqbal did not write a verse-by-verse commentary, and he was a poet rather than a trained mufassir. Yet his lectures shaped how educated South Asian Muslims, and later many others, thought about the text. Fazlur Rahman took up his call for a new ijtihad; Islamists borrowed his praise of action; Sufis claimed his love of Rumi. His verse is recited at gatherings across Pakistan and India, and lines of it are quoted in the Qur'an classes of Chicago's South Asian mosques.

words.d: poet and philosopher of Lahore (1877–1938) whose Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam urged a dynamic reading of the Qur'an
Iqbal's 1930 lectures calling for Muslims to rethink their religious ideas with modern knowledge
marked by movement and change; Iqbal's word for the Qur'an's spirit

lessons.title: Women Reading the Qur'an
lessons.mainIdea: Amina Wadud and Asma Barlas argued that the Qur'an read as a whole supports the equality of women and that classical readings reflected their male authors' world.
reading: Women have taught the Qur'an since the first generation. Muslim tradition names Aisha, the Prophet's wife, as a leading source of hadith and interpretation, and the biographies of scholars list many women who taught men. But the great written commentaries were all by men, and the law schools were built by men. In the late twentieth century, women trained in universities began to write commentary of their own and to ask what difference that made.

Amina Wadud, an American convert, published Qur'an and Woman in Malaysia in 1992. Her method borrows from Fazlur Rahman. She reads each verse about women in its context, asks what principle it served, and then reads it against the Qur'an's overall picture of humanity, which she argues is one of equal moral agents created from a single soul, as Surah al-Nisa (4), ayah 1, says. Asma Barlas, in Believing Women in Islam (2002), argued further that a God the Qur'an describes as just cannot be read as endorsing injustice, so any reading that subordinates women must be a misreading.

The hardest test case is Surah al-Nisa (4), ayah 34. It describes men as maintainers or protectors of women, ties this to what men spend, and gives a sequence of steps for a husband who fears rebellion from his wife, the last of which uses the verb daraba, most often translated to strike. Classical commentators read the verse as permitting a light blow and limited it heavily. Wadud reads the verse as describing, not commanding, a seventh-century arrangement, and as restricting an existing practice. Some modern translators render daraba as to separate from or to go away from, a reading most classical grammarians did not adopt. Wadud has said that she ultimately refuses the verse's plain sense as a moral guide, a position that other Muslim women scholars, including those who defend the classical readings, have criticized.

These debates go on in universities, in mosques and online, in English, Arabic, Indonesian and Persian. Some Muslim women scholars argue instead from within the classical law schools, finding room for women there. Others reject the whole project as importing Western ideas. Historians of the field note that what is new is not women reading the Qur'an, which is old, but women publishing commentaries under their own names and being answered as commentators.

words.d: American scholar whose Qur'an and Woman (1992) reads the text for the equality of women; she led a mixed Friday prayer in 2005
scholar whose Believing Women in Islam (2002) argues that a just God cannot be read as endorsing injustice against women
the Prophet's wife, named in Muslim tradition as a major source of hadith and early interpretation
the Arabic verb in 4:34 usually translated to strike; its meaning in that verse is disputed by modern readers

lessons.title: Science in the Text
lessons.mainIdea: Scientific exegesis claims the Qur'an anticipates modern discoveries; its Muslim critics say the text is guidance, not a science book, and that tying it to today's theories is risky.
reading: Open a website or a pamphlet on Islam and science and you may find a list: the Qur'an on the expanding universe, on the water cycle, on the stages of the embryo, on the barrier between two seas. This approach is called *tafsir ilmi*, scientific exegesis. Its claim is that the Qur'an mentions facts no seventh-century person could have known, and that this proves its divine origin. The approach is old in seed, since al-Ghazali and al-Razi both held that the Qur'an contains all knowledge in principle, but it grew large in the twentieth century.

The Egyptian scholar Tantawi Jawhari (d. 1940) wrote a multi-volume commentary filled with diagrams, plant lists and scientific tables, arguing that Muslims had neglected the hundreds of verses about nature. In 1976 a French physician, Maurice Bucaille, published a book arguing that the Qur'an, unlike the Bible, contained no statement at odds with modern science. Bucaille's book was translated widely and is still handed out. Verses such as Surah al-Anbiya (21), ayah 30, which says the heavens and the earth were one piece and God split them apart and made every living thing from water, are quoted as forecasts of cosmology and biology.

The critics are mostly Muslims. The Egyptian scholar Amin al-Khuli (d. 1966) argued that the Qur'an spoke to its first audience in the language and science of their day, and that reading modern theories into it distorts both the text and the science. Others note the risk: if a verse is tied to today's theory, what happens when the theory changes? Scientists who are Muslims have pointed out that the verses are read after the discovery, never before it, so they predict nothing. The classical commentators, they add, read 21:30 as a statement about God's creative power, not as astronomy.

A middle position is common in mosques and classrooms. On this view the Qur'an invites study of nature, as 2:164 and many other verses say, and a believer may see harmony between faith and science without claiming the text contains equations. The debate is worth knowing because it shows how a modern pressure, the prestige of science, produced a new way of reading, and how the tradition's own tools, context and the plain sense, were used to push back.

words.d: scientific exegesis: reading the Qur'an as anticipating modern scientific discoveries
Egyptian scholar (d. 1940) whose commentary filled the text with scientific tables and diagrams
French physician whose 1976 book argued the Qur'an agrees with modern science; widely reprinted
Egyptian scholar (d. 1966) who argued the Qur'an speaks in the language of its first audience, not modern science

look.title: A Verse and a Theory
look.text: Surah al-Anbiya (21), ayah 30, asks whether the disbelievers have not seen that the heavens and the earth were joined together and God parted them, and that God made every living thing from water. A scientific exegete says: this is the Big Bang and the water basis of life. A critic says: the classical commentators read it as God's power in creation, and a seventh-century listener heard rain parting the sky from a dry earth. The physicist in the room says: a verse read after a discovery predicts nothing.
look.prompt: Lay out the three positions fairly. Which of the commentator's classical tools does the critic use? What would count as evidence for or against the exegete's claim?

That the Qur'an should be read only by scientists
That science and the Qur'an have nothing to say to each other
That the Qur'an forbids the study of nature
check.why: Scientific exegesis reads the Qur'an as anticipating modern discoveries; its critics dispute both the method and the claim.

check.q: What was Amin al-Khuli's main objection to scientific exegesis?
choices: That the Qur'an was not in Arabic
That science is forbidden in Islam
That the Qur'an spoke in the language and knowledge of its first audience, so reading modern theories into it distorts it
That only al-Razi may discuss nature
check.why: Al-Khuli argued from context: the text addressed seventh-century listeners, and importing later science misreads it.

check.q: Why do some Muslim scientists say the scientific readings predict nothing?
choices: Because the Qur'an has no verses about nature
Because the verses are matched to theories only after the discovery is made
Because the Qur'an was written after modern science
Because scientists never read the Qur'an
check.why: The critics note that verses are read as forecasts only in hindsight, and that tying a verse to a theory risks the theory changing.

sections.title: The Qur'an in English and Online

lessons.title: The Translation Debate
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims have long held that the Qur'an is untranslatable in the full sense, so English versions are called meanings or interpretations, and each one makes choices readers should notice.
reading: Most Muslims hold that the Qur'an is the Qur'an only in Arabic. A version in another language is a *translation of the meanings*, useful for understanding but not the text itself, and it is not used for ritual prayer. This view goes back to the classical scholars and their doctrine of i'jaz, the text's inimitable eloquence. It explains why English versions carry titles like The Meaning of the Glorious Koran or The Koran Interpreted, and why a printed translation almost always has the Arabic beside it.

The English history begins with outsiders. George Sale, an English lawyer, published a translation in 1734 with a long introduction; it was read by Voltaire and Jefferson and shaped European views for a century. J. M. Rodwell (1861) rearranged the surahs into what he thought was their order of revelation. E. H. Palmer (1880), a Cambridge scholar of Arabic, aimed at plain, sometimes rough, English. All three were Christians writing for non-Muslim readers, and Muslims noted the distance in their tone.

Marmaduke Pickthall, an English novelist who became a Muslim, published The Meaning of the Glorious Koran in 1930 with the approval of scholars at al-Azhar. His stately, King James-style English is the version this course quotes. Abdullah Yusuf Ali, an Indian civil servant, followed in 1934 with a translation in verse-like lines and thousands of notes; it became the most widely distributed English Qur'an of the twentieth century. A. J. Arberry, a British scholar, tried in 1955 to carry the sound and rhythm of the Arabic into English. Since then Muslim translators such as Muhammad Asad (1980) and M. A. S. Abdel Haleem (2004) have written in modern prose, and The Study Quran (2015) added a commentary drawn from the classical tradition.

Each translator made choices. Should Allah be rendered as God? Pickthall kept Allah; Abdel Haleem writes God. Should the difficult verb in 4:34 be to strike, to beat lightly, or something else? Should the reader see the surahs in the traditional order or Rodwell's? Should the notes lean Sunni, Shia, modernist or Sufi? Comparing two translations of one verse is one of the best ways to see how interpretation works, because every translation is already a reading.

words.d: the Muslim description of a Qur'an in another language: an aid to understanding, not the text itself
English novelist and Muslim whose 1930 translation, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, is quoted in this course
Abdullah Yusuf Ali, whose 1934 translation with extensive notes became the most distributed English Qur'an of the twentieth century
A. J. Arberry, British scholar whose 1955 The Koran Interpreted tried to carry the Arabic's rhythm into English

Because most Muslims hold that the Qur'an is fully the Qur'an only in Arabic
Because the translators did not know Arabic
Because the law requires that title
check.why: The doctrine of i'jaz holds the Arabic text to be inimitable, so a version in another language conveys meanings but is not the text.

choices: George Sale
Marmaduke Pickthall
J. M. Rodwell
Yusuf Ali
check.why: Rodwell's 1861 translation reordered the surahs chronologically as he judged it; the others kept the traditional order.

choices: Yusuf Ali, 1934
Arberry, 1955

lessons.title: The Qur'an on a Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Websites and apps have put the Arabic text, recitations, many translations and classical commentaries in every pocket, changing how people study and who can weigh in.
reading: A student in Chicago today can open a phone, tap a verse, hear it recited by a dozen reciters, see six translations side by side, read al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir in English, and look up the grammar of every word. Twenty years ago that would have taken a research library and a knowledge of Arabic. Sites and apps that offer the text with translations and audio, and a word-by-word grammatical corpus built at a British university, are now the everyday tools of study for millions.

Historians of religion see three effects. First, access: people who could never read a classical commentary now can, in their own language. Second, comparison: seeing translations side by side shows readers that translation is interpretation, a lesson that once took years of study. Third, a flattening of authority: a video by a popular preacher and a page from al-Razi appear on the same screen with equal weight. The reader must decide what to trust, which is exactly the problem the classical scholars built their chains of transmission to solve.

The internet also revived old debates in new forms. Disputes over a verse now unfold in comment threads across continents. Scientific exegesis spreads by short videos. So do rebuttals. Groups that reject the whole hadith tradition, and read the Qur'an alone, have found an audience online that they never had in print. So have traditional scholars who post lectures on the classical texts. Scholars of Islam in America note that many young Muslims now first meet tafsir on a screen rather than in a mosque.

None of this changed the text. The Arabic on the screen is the 1924 Cairo edition, and the recitations follow the same rules of *tajwid* that a tenth-century reciter used. What changed is the room the text sits in: bigger, noisier, and open to anyone. That is the modern version of the question this unit began with. Who interprets, and by what method, and how does a reader tell good interpretation from bad?

words.d: a searchable body of text; the Quranic Arabic Corpus tags every word's grammar
the rules for reciting the Qur'an correctly, unchanged by the move to audio and apps
the standing to have one's reading trusted; the internet has flattened it

look.title: Six Windows, One Verse
look.text: A reader opens an app to Surah al-Fatiha (1), ayah 5, and sees six English versions of the same line side by side. Some say Thee alone we worship; some say You alone we worship; some add and from You alone we seek help, others say ask for help. Below them sits a video from a popular preacher, and below that, a passage from Ibn Kathir in translation.
look.prompt: What can the reader learn from the six versions that a single printed translation would hide? What should the reader ask before trusting the video or the medieval commentary?

check.q: Which effect of the internet do historians of religion describe as a flattening of authority?
choices: Reciters no longer follow tajwid
The Arabic text has changed on screens
A popular video and a classical commentary appear with equal weight, so the reader must judge
Translations are no longer available
check.why: Online, sources of very different standing sit side by side, which puts the burden of judging trust on the reader.

check.q: What did NOT change when the Qur'an moved to screens?
choices: The Arabic text and the rules of recitation
The number of people who can read a commentary
The ease of comparing translations
The reach of popular preachers
check.why: The text on screens is the 1924 Cairo edition, and recitation still follows tajwid; access, comparison and reach are what changed.

check.q: What lesson does seeing translations side by side teach a reader?
choices: That the Qur'an was written in English
That translation is itself an act of interpretation
That only one translation is correct
That the surahs are in the wrong order
check.why: Comparison shows that every translation makes choices, a point that once took years of study to learn.

lessons.title: Reading in America
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims in the United States, diverse in origin and school, read the Qur'an in many ways, and the story of that reading in Chicago goes back to 1893.
reading: Estimates vary, but surveys by the Pew Research Center put the number of Muslims in the United States at about 3.5 million in 2017, a little over one percent of the population, and growing. No single origin dominates. Roughly a fifth of American Muslims are Black Americans, many of whose families entered Islam in the twentieth century; large groups trace their roots to South Asia, the Arab world, Iran, Africa and Southeast Asia; and a share are converts. Most are Sunni, a smaller share Shia, and many decline any label. That diversity means American Muslims bring nearly every reading tradition in this unit to the same text.

Chicago's part of the story is old. At the World's Parliament of Religions, held in Chicago in 1893 alongside the World's Columbian Exposition, an American convert named Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb spoke about Islam to a mostly Christian audience, one of the first public presentations of the religion by a Muslim in the United States. In the twentieth century, Chicago became a center of Black American Islam, and the city and its suburbs now hold dozens of mosques serving Arab, South Asian, Bosnian, Turkish, African and American-born congregations, along with Islamic schools and a college of Islamic studies.

How do these communities read? A Friday sermon in a South Asian mosque may quote Maududi; an Arab mosque may quote Ibn Kathir; a Sufi gathering may read al-Qushayri; a university study group may argue about Fazlur Rahman or Amina Wadud. Weekend Qur'an schools teach children to recite with tajwid, and some produce huffaz, students who have memorized the whole text, by the age of twelve. Public-school students study the Qur'an in world history and, as here, in courses on religious texts, using the same tools scholars use.

Surveys of American Muslims find that most say the Qur'an should be read with attention to its context and that there is more than one true way to interpret Islam, though a large minority holds that it should be read literally. What almost all share is the sense, expressed by the Qur'an in Surah al-Baqara (2), ayah 2, that the book is a guidance for those who are mindful, and the conviction that the Arabic, recited, is where the text lives. A student in Illinois who has followed this unit can now hear that recitation, read the classical debates, and understand why the same verse sounds different in different rooms.

words.d: a nonpartisan research organization whose surveys are a common source for estimates of religious populations
a gathering of religious leaders in Chicago in 1893 at which Islam was presented by an American convert
plural of hafiz: people who have memorized the whole Qur'an
variety of origin, school and reading among a community; a mark of Muslims in the United States

An American convert, Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb, presented Islam to a largely Christian audience

choices: Only one commentary is allowed in the United States
Most American Muslims read the Qur'an only in English
The Qur'an is not recited in American mosques

check.why: Communities of different origin and school quote Maududi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qushayri or Rahman, bringing the whole range of readings to one text.

review.q: Which 1924 event gave most of the Muslim world its standard printed Qur'an?
choices: Pickthall's translation
The Egyptian government's Cairo edition
The founding of al-Manar
Maududi's commentary
review.why: The Cairo edition of 1924, following the reading of Hafs from Asim, became the standard text; Pickthall's translation came in 1930.

review.q: Which two men are the authors of Tafsir al-Manar?
choices: Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida
Sayyid Qutb and Maududi
Fazlur Rahman and Iqbal
Pickthall and Yusuf Ali
review.why: Abduh's al-Azhar lectures, printed and continued by Rida in the journal al-Manar, make up Tafsir al-Manar.

review.q: What is Fazlur Rahman's double movement?
choices: Reading the Qur'an twice, once in Arabic and once in English
Reciting a verse forward and backward
Comparing Sunni and Shia commentaries on every verse
Going from the present to the original context to find a principle, then applying it to today
review.why: Rahman's two steps find the moral aim of a ruling in its seventh-century setting and then bring that aim to modern conditions.

review.q: How did Qutb extend the word jahiliyya?
choices: To the science of recitation
To the age of the Companions
To modern societies not ruled by God's law
To the pre-Islamic poets only
review.why: Classically jahiliyya names pre-Islamic Arabia; Qutb applied it to his own society, which many Muslim scholars rejected.

review.q: What is the main claim of scientific exegesis, tafsir ilmi?
choices: That the Qur'an forbids science
That the Qur'an anticipates modern discoveries, proving its divine origin
That the Qur'an was written by scientists
That science disproves the Qur'an
review.why: Tafsir ilmi reads the Qur'an as forecasting modern findings; critics such as Amin al-Khuli argue it speaks in its first audience's terms.

review.q: Which translator became a Muslim and published The Meaning of the Glorious Koran in 1930?
choices: Marmaduke Pickthall
George Sale
A. J. Arberry
E. H. Palmer
review.why: Pickthall, an English novelist and convert, published his translation in 1930 with al-Azhar's approval; Sale, Palmer and Arberry were not Muslims.

review.q: Who spoke about Islam at the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago?
choices: Muhammad Abduh
Fazlur Rahman
Muhammad Iqbal
Mohammed Alexander Russell Webb
review.why: Webb, an American convert, presented Islam at the 1893 Parliament; Abduh, Iqbal and Rahman were never there.

review.q: What does Amina Wadud argue about Surah al-Nisa 4:34?
choices: That the verse is not in the Qur'an
That it should be read only in Arabic
That it describes and restricts a seventh-century arrangement, read against the Qur'an's picture of equal souls
That it was written by Ibn Kathir
review.why: Wadud reads 4:34 in context and against 4:1, treating it as descriptive and limiting rather than as a command.
